extracted.intended_audience: natural philosophers / experimental investigators (practitioners of empirical inquiry)
extracted.subtask_description: Practical methodological guidance for discovering natures and causes in natural philosophy by means of carefully chosen instances, discriminating experiments, and instruments that reduce hidden phenomena to the senses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Instances of the Cross
rubrics_metrics.description: Instances which pit two rival suppositions against each other so as to decide between them; they 'cross' alternative explanations and allow one to be adopted or another suspected.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design experiments or seek occurrences that would happen under one hypothesis but not the other. Examples given: (a) historical/comparative instance — if any comet revolved not in harmony with diurnal motion, allow such motion possible; (b) gravity — compare whether weight varies with distance (clock-atop-church vs clock-in-mine experiment) to test attraction by the earth’s mass; (c) magnetism — place a magnetic globe E–W and an untouched needle above it for days, then see whether the needle returns to N–S when removed (if it does, earth-caused polarity is indicated); (d) reflection by rare bodies — test whether flames of sufficient depth reflect light (sun's rays through a hole on a bluish flame); (e) projectile motion — test whether air carries projectiles (stream-behind-boat model) or internal succession pushes them (bent plate/reed leap experiment); (f) gunpowder explosion — distinguish expansion of flame from escape of a crude spirit (compare behaviour of sulphur/camphor mixtures, salts, quicksilver); (g) flame continuity — color-separated flame-in-flame experiment to see if an enclosed flame continues as the same mass or is regenerated. Use such cross-instances to decide between candidate causes rather than rely on probable reasons.

rubrics_metrics.name: Instances of Divorce
rubrics_metrics.description: Instances showing the separation of a particular nature from a concrete substance with which it is commonly conjoined; they indicate that two natures can exist apart.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use cases that demonstrate that commonly-associated qualities are separable. Examples: air is rare and mobile but neither hot nor light; the moon is light but not hot; boiling water warm but not light; compass motion (magnetism) occurs in cold, dense, opaque bodies. Such instances help expose false generalizations and show that apparent associations do not prove necessary connection. They also serve to test whether an action (e.g., magnetic attraction) can exist independently of a corporeal medium, bearing on questions of incorporeal power.

rubrics_metrics.name: Instances of the Lamp (immediate information)
rubrics_metrics.description: Classes of instances that 'assist the senses' and thus lead from sensory perception to true notions; they make sensory data more abundant and accurate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Five uses are enumerated: (1) strengthen, enlarge, and correct senses; (2) reduce to the sphere of the senses matters beyond ordinary perception; (3) indicate continued processes or series of motions only ordinarily seen in their termination; (4) supply absolute wants of the senses; (5) excite attention and limit subtleties. Prioritize collecting and improving sensory data because interpretation begins with the senses rather than probable reasons.

rubrics_metrics.name: Instances of the Door or Gate (assistance to the senses)
rubrics_metrics.description: Instances and instruments that enable the senses either to perceive objects not naturally seen, to see them from greater distance, or to see them more accurately and distinctly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Threefold assistance: (a) reveal hidden things (microscope); (b) extend sight to remote objects (telescope); (c) increase accuracy and correction (measuring rods, astrolabes). Examples and cautions: microscopes disclose minute structure (flea, animalculæ) but are inadequate for larger bodies; telescopes reveal new stellar facts (Milky Way knots, Jupiter's satellites, lunar irregularities) but single-method discoveries must be regarded cautiously; measuring devices correct and guide sight and should be used when they add genuine information.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of Microscopes: perception of minute structure
rubrics_metrics.description: Employ microscopes to exhibit latent and invisible minutiæ and hidden motions of substances to strengthen and enlarge sight.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Microscopes are useful for very minute objects (flea, moss, animalculæ, irregularities of pen lines). Note their inadequacy for larger bodies and beware of over-extending their interpretations; improvements that scale up such revelation would be highly valuable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of Telescopes: reduction of distance
rubrics_metrics.description: Use telescopes to bring distant objects into sensory reach and to observe phenomena otherwise inaccessible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Telescope examples include resolving the Milky Way into stars, seeing moons of Jupiter, lunar surface irregularities, sunspots. Treat novel telescope-based claims with caution if they rest on few instances; corroboration and further application to other worthy objects are required before confident conclusions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of Corrective Measuring Instruments (measuring rods, astrolabes)
rubrics_metrics.description: Apply measuring and corrective instruments to guide and correct sensory observation so it becomes more accurate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use such instruments when they do not simply enlarge sight but correct it; they belong among door/gate instances and serve to make observations reliable and reproducible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Citing/Invoking Instances (reduce invisible phenomena to the senses)
rubrics_metrics.description: Instances that 'cite' or invoke phenomena so as to reduce objects not immediately within the senses into the sphere of sensory observation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Objects escape the senses by distance, interposition, insufficiency of quantity, too short or too long timescale, violent impression, or sensory saturation. Reduction strategies include: substituting a perceivable signal at distance (beacons, bells); using surface signs to reveal hidden interior states (pulse, urine); observing secondary effects (rust, desiccation, change of weight) to infer invisible spirit/activity; creating separations or distillations to render constituents perceptible; and slowing or prolonging processes to make them sensible. These methods are essential for investigating air, spirit, subtle tissues, and beginnings of life.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reduction by Artificial Separation and Distillation (with caution)
rubrics_metrics.description: Render mixtures and invisible constituents sensible by skilful artificial separations (distillation, separation of aqueous/oily/spirituous parts).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such separations can reveal how much of butter/cheese/whey in milk or quantify constituents, but one must beware that violent methods (strong heat, energetic agents) may superinduce new qualities and produce artifacts (e.g., vapor created by fire that was not present). Prefer gentler methods that imitate nature; always consider whether the separation method itself introduces fallacies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of Weight and Tables to Assess Density and Quantity of Matter
rubrics_metrics.description: Weighing and compiling comparative tables to determine the relative quantity of matter in different bodies and thereby infer density/rarity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Weight is proportionate to the quantity of tangible matter; assemble tables of weights for metals, minerals, liquids, etc., to reveal proportions and unexpected results (Bacon's table suggests the familiar range is within a ratio of 1:21). Use weighing to detect changes (e.g., diminution of weight upon emission of 'spirit').

rubrics_metrics.name: Experimental measurement of gaseous expansion (vapor quantification)
rubrics_metrics.description: Quantify expansion when a tangible body is converted into an aëriform state to compare volumes of tangible vs intangible bodies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example experiment: heat a small vial of spirits of wine inside a bladder, exhaust the air, capture the vapor expansion, then weigh remaining spirit to estimate how much converted to vapor and compare occupied space; Bacon reports ~100× expansion. Such contrivances reduce pneumatic bodies to measurable terms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of Thermometers to Render Heat/Cold Sensible
rubrics_metrics.description: Use a thermometer (or air-expansion device) to make otherwise insensible degrees of heat or cold perceptible by reduction to visible movement (e.g., water depression/raising).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Heat expands and cold contracts air; the air’s expansion/contraction can be rendered visible by water movement, thereby making small thermal differences perceptible. Employ instruments that convert thermal change into visible motion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Design discriminating experiments for questions of projectile motion
rubrics_metrics.description: Construct experiments that distinguish whether projectile motion is caused by the surrounding air carrying the body or by successive internal motion of the projectile's parts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not accept scholastic axioms without test. Bacon recommends experiments like bending and releasing a thin stiff plate or split reed between finger and thumb to see a centre-sourced leap which cannot be due to air collecting behind the object; such tests localize the source of motion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Design discriminating experiments for explosive forces (gunpowder)
rubrics_metrics.description: Differentiate whether explosive violence is due simply to expansion of flame or to escape/expansion of a 'crude spirit' (vapor) assisting flame.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compare outcomes of very inflammable substances (sulphur, camphor, naphtha) which ignite readily but do not produce the same violence as gunpowder, and substances that repel flame (salts) which emit aqueous spirits before flame. Quicksilver’s explosive expansion is cited. The correct experiment must show whether the violence arises from generation plus escape of a spirit or merely from flame expansion; control for suppression of flame by confining mass to see whether flame generation is impeded.

rubrics_metrics.name: Design experiments probing the transitory nature of flame
rubrics_metrics.description: Test whether a flame is a continuous identical mass or a succession of momentary generations extinguished and regenerated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Observe large conflagrations (pyramidal flame form) and design tests such as placing a yellow taper and surrounding blue spirit flame in a basin to see whether the enclosed flame remains pyramidal or becomes globular; if the enclosed colour-distinguishable flame remains, this suggests flame continuity when not exposed to compressing air; otherwise flame is momentary. Use observations of shape (pyramid vs inverted pyramid for smoke) to infer dynamics of destruction by air at sides and persistence at center.

rubrics_metrics.name: Observe rudiments/beginnings for vital processes
rubrics_metrics.description: Infer processes of life and organic formation by diligent observation of first beginnings, rudiments, and early effects (e.g., animalculæ from putrefaction).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Look to the earliest stages (eggs of ants, worms, mosses, frogs after rain) and mild heat plus pliant substrate are necessary; the gradual formation distinguishes retained/expanded spirit vs emitted spirit. Such observations reduce subtle formative processes to sensory evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Infer hidden spirits/actions from indirect signs
rubrics_metrics.description: When a spirit or non-tangible action cannot be perceived directly, infer its presence from indirect, measurable signs such as diminution of weight, rust, desiccation, contraction, fissures, softening, or flow.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: desiccation accompanied by loss in quantity indicates emission of spirit; rust and putrefaction show emission; softened metals or flowing of gums indicate spirit retained and excited. Use these indirect effects as proxies for invisible processes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Account for limitations of the senses in timescale and intensity
rubrics_metrics.description: Recognize that sensory perception operates by motion (time); very slow or very rapid motions may escape direct perception and must be rendered observable by devices or substitutions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: hour-hand motion (too slow) and musket-ball flight (too fast) both escape ordinary perception; design instruments or methods that slow, extend, or otherwise render such motions sensible (time-reduction devices, signals).

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer experimental instances over probable reasons
rubrics_metrics.description: Give priority to actual instances and enlightening experiments rather than probable reasoning or scholastic disputation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Bacon repeatedly emphasizes that judgments of nature must be taught by instances and experiments (which enlighten and accustom mankind to judge nature) rather than by probable reasons or abstruse scholastic theory. Collect multiple, varied instances and perform discriminating experiments rather than rely on authority or opaque argument.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use historical and credible occurrences as instances when available
rubrics_metrics.description: Employ trustworthy historical reports or observed occurrences as instances to permit or refute natural possibilities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a trustworthy history reports a phenomenon (e.g., a comet not following diurnal motion), accept that as evidence to allow a motion in nature; absence of such histories should direct inquiry to other cross-instances. Always assess credibility of reports.
